title: The Cyberbullying Dilemma
setup: It's late at night in your first-year hall. Your phone buzzes. It's the department group.
contentNote: This scene shows online harassment. The edited image is never shown.

questions.prompt: Tanvir Bhai says: share it in your batch group, or forget about senior support for finals. What do you do?

tag.label: Resisting peer pressure
tag.strength: You don't let pressure make your choices for you.
tag.growth: Practise saying no, especially when it costs you something.

options.text: Share it in the batch group. Senior support really matters for finals.
options.shift: Within an hour, 300 people had seen it. Nusrat skipped her lab exam the next morning.

options.text: Don't share it, but drop a 😂 so the seniors stay on your side.
options.shift: Your emoji told 214 people this was funny. Nusrat saw your name in the reactions.

options.text: Refuse, delete it, and privately tell him spreading edited photos is a crime.
options.shift: The chain stopped with you. Nusrat's batch never saw it from your phone.

options.text: Forward it to just one close friend and ask what they think.
options.shift: Your friend forwarded it 'just once' too. That is how every viral post starts.

questions.prompt: The meme is already in the department group and 40 people have seen it. What's the most responsible next step?

tag.label: Active bystander
tag.strength: You act when you see harm happening.
tag.growth: Silence and side-fights both help harm spread. Report it instead.

options.text: Stay quiet. It's not your business and others will deal with it.
options.shift: Silence looked like agreement. The post stayed up for three days.

options.text: Report the post and ask the group admin privately to remove it.
options.shift: The admin removed it within the hour. Far fewer people saw it.

options.text: Reply in the group calling Tanvir Bhai out with harsh words.
options.shift: The fight got 60 replies, and the meme got more attention than before.

options.text: Screenshot it and post it on your story to expose the senior.
options.shift: You meant to help, but now Nusrat's image is on your story too.

questions.prompt: Nusrat hasn't come to class for two days. What do you do?

tag.label: Supporting the person harmed
tag.strength: You reach out to people who are hurting.
tag.growth: One kind message can change someone's whole week.

options.text: Leave her alone. She probably wants space right now.
options.shift: She felt the whole batch had turned on her. No one checked in.

options.text: Message her that it wasn't okay, and offer to help her report it.
options.shift: One message made her feel less alone. She reported it the next day.

options.text: Ask in the class group whether the photo was really her.
options.shift: Your question pulled the meme back into everyone's attention.

options.text: Tell her to delete her social media so it all goes away.
options.shift: She vanished from her own online life while the person who did it carried on.

questions.prompt: Tanvir Bhai finds out you refused. He messages: "Don't expect any help from us." What do you do?

tag.label: Standing firm without revenge
tag.strength: You hold your ground without hitting back.
tag.growth: Revenge and public shaming restart the cycle of harm.

options.text: Apologise and share the meme after all, just to fix things.
options.shift: You got the notes back. Nusrat got another wave of cruel messages.

options.text: Keep your decision, study with classmates, and tell your adviser if it continues.
options.shift: Two classmates said they had refused too. You weren't alone.

options.text: Make a meme about Tanvir Bhai to get back at him.
options.shift: Now there were two victims, and the cycle kept going.

options.text: Post the whole story publicly with his name to shame him.
options.shift: It went viral, and it dragged Nusrat's name back into it too.

help.title: If this happens to you or a friend
lines: Save evidence privately. Don't forward it.
Report the post on the platform.
Talk to someone you trust: a friend, teacher, adviser or proctor.
In Bangladesh: call 999 in an emergency, or 109 (helpline for violence against women and children).
